n.4: A shade guide is used for colour selection.
n.3: An impression tray carries impression material, not carious tissue.

10.q: A bottle cap is left loose on etching gel. What error should be recognised?
o: Container not secured, increasing spill or exposure risk
10.w: Poorly secured containers may leak, spill or expose staff to hazardous substances.

n.4: Stock level is not the main issue.
n.2: Label clarity is beneficial.
n.3: Room brightness is unrelated.
n.1: Bottle size is not the principal error.

10.q: Using the image, identify item number 6.
10.w: Item 6 is a removable partial denture with clasps.

n.2: Night guards cover occlusal surfaces differently.
n.0: Bleaching trays are thin transparent trays.
n.3: Orthodontic retainers differ in design.
n.1: A mouth prop is not a prosthesis.

10.q: Several panoramic images in one session show the same blurred appearance as this example. Which scenario is the most likely explanation?
o: Patients are not being stabilised or instructed adequately before exposure
The developer solution has been freshly changed
The operator repeatedly selects adult exposure settings
The surgery lighting is too bright
10.w: Repeated movement blur usually indicates a workflow issue with positioning, stabilisation or patient instructions.

n.3: Exposure settings mainly affect density and noise rather than repeated motion blur.
n.4: Room lighting does not cause panoramic movement artefact.
n.2: Fresh chemicals do not create this type of blur.
n.1: Disposable bite blocks are unrelated to this recurring error.

10.q: A nurse is explaining to a patient how decay develops if left untreated. Which sequence best describes the progression of dental caries?
10.w: Caries progresses from enamel to dentine and then to the pulp.

n.0: Caries begins in enamel, not dentine.
n.4: Pulp involvement occurs last.
n.3: Pulp is not affected before dentine.
n.1: Enamel is always first affected.

10.q: A patient is being fitted with a new partial denture. What is the main purpose of clasp arms on many partial dentures?
10.w: Clasps help retain the denture by engaging suitable tooth contours.

n.4: Clasps do not whiten teeth.
n.1: Pocket depth is measured with probes.
n.3: They do not record jaw size.
n.2: They are unrelated to burs.

10.q: Which interpretation of the white and red areas within the lesion shown in the image is most appropriate?
o: They are typical of a normal fungiform papilla pattern
They indicate simple dehydration of the tongue
They may represent dysplastic or malignant surface change within a suspicious ulcer
They show healing granulation tissue after a recent extraction
They suggest a harmless tongue coating only
10.w: Mixed red and white change within a persistent irregular ulcer is suspicious and may represent dysplastic or malignant epithelial change.

n.4: A harmless tongue coating would not usually appear as part of an irregular ulcerated lesion.
n.1: Dehydration does not explain this focal destructive lesion.
n.3: Granulation tissue after extraction would not occur at this site or have this appearance.
n.0: Normal papillae do not present as mixed red-white ulceration.

10.q: A domestic bin contains partially used chemicals from cleaning. What should be recognised?
o: An acceptable practice if the containers are sealed
Correct disposal provided the chemicals are diluted
Potentially incorrect disposal of hazardous waste
Reasonable if the product is no longer in use
Routine disposal that only needs recording in the waste log
10.w: Some chemicals require specific disposal routes and should not automatically enter domestic waste.

n.0: A sealed container in a domestic bin is still the wrong waste stream.
n.1: Dilution does not change how a hazardous substance must be disposed of.
n.3: Being out of use does not make it safe to bin.
n.4: Recording the wrong disposal route does not make it right.

10.q: Using the image, which item best represents processed instruments ready for use?
10.w: Sealed pouches indicate instruments that have been packaged and processed for use.

n.0: Open dirty trays contain contaminated instruments.
n.3: Sink contents are unprocessed items.
n.4: Used gloves are waste.
n.2: Sharps waste is not reusable equipment.

10.q: A patient is due to begin a course of treatment and the consent form is being completed. Which statement best describes valid consent in dental care?
o: It can be given by any relative
It is given only in writing
It is only needed for surgical treatment
It is voluntary, informed and given by a person with capacity
10.w: Valid consent should be given freely, based on adequate information, by someone with capacity to decide.

n.1: Consent may be verbal, written or implied depending on circumstances.
n.4: Consent can be withdrawn and may need reconfirmation.
n.2: Consent applies to many forms of treatment, not only surgery.
n.0: Relatives cannot automatically consent for competent adults.

10.q: A completed denture has arrived back from the laboratory. Before fitting a new denture, what should the dental nurse confirm first?
10.w: Confirming the correct patient and appliance is a key safety check before fitting.

n.4: Clean shade tabs are useful but not the first priority.
n.2: Bowls are unrelated to immediate fitting.
n.3: Brush replacement is not the primary check.
n.0: Articulator screws are laboratory concerns.

10.q: A staff member handles patient notes while wearing contaminated gloves. What is the main concern?
10.w: Contaminated gloves can transfer microorganisms to frequently touched non-clinical surfaces.

n.0: The infection risk is more significant than smudging.
n.3: Speed of writing is not the main issue.
n.1: Handling notes does not inherently lose records.
n.2: Paper damage is secondary to contamination risk.

10.q: A periapical radiograph of the lower right posterior region shows the root apices positioned very close to the image edge. What is the main concern with this image?
o: The exposure is too dark to identify the crowns
The image is unsuitable because only one tooth should be visible
The teeth appear elongated due to excessive vertical angulation
There is a risk that apical pathology may be missed because the apices are inadequately captured
There is clear cone cut affecting the crowns
10.w: Periapical radiographs should include the entire root and surrounding apical bone. When apices are at the edge, diagnostic information may be incomplete.

n.0: Overall density is acceptable and crowns remain visible.
n.2: Tooth length appears generally normal rather than clearly elongated.
n.4: Cone cut would show an unexposed white area, which is not present.
n.1: Multiple teeth are commonly included on posterior periapical views.

10.q: During quality assurance review, several bitewings show errors similar to the image. Which scenario is the most likely underlying cause?
o: The lead apron collar is positioned too high
The operator consistently aims the beam from too far mesially or distally
The processor temperature is too high
The X-ray tubehead drifts downward after positioning
10.w: Repeated overlap across multiple images usually indicates a consistent horizontal angulation error by the operator.

n.4: Tubehead droop may alter vertical angulation more than consistent contact overlap.
n.3: Processing temperature affects image density and contrast.
n.0: Swallowing may cause motion blur rather than overlap.
n.1: A high thyroid collar may obscure anterior anatomy, not create posterior overlap.

10.q: During manual cleaning of instruments, splashing is likely. Which PPE combination is most appropriate?
o: Disposable gloves, eye protection, fluid-resistant mask and apron
Heavy-duty gloves and eye protection only
Heavy-duty gloves, eye protection, fluid-resistant mask and apron
Heavy-duty gloves, visor and apron only
Visor, fluid-resistant mask and disposable gloves
10.w: Manual cleaning with splash risk requires protection for hands, eyes, respiratory area and clothing.

n.0: Correct in every respect except the gloves: thin examination gloves tear on sharp instruments, so HTM 01-05 specifies heavy-duty gloves for manual cleaning.
n.1: Protects hands and eyes but leaves the face and clothing exposed to splashing.
n.3: A visor shields the face but is not a substitute for a fluid-resistant mask.
n.4: Face and clothing are covered but disposable gloves give no puncture protection during scrubbing.

10.q: A composite restoration appears lighter after dehydration from prolonged rubber dam isolation. What is the best action before final shade judgement?
o: Rehydrate teeth and reassess shade later
10.w: Dehydrated teeth look lighter; rehydration can alter apparent shade.

n.4: Immediate replacement may be unnecessary.
n.1: Curing time does not correct dehydration colour change.
n.2: Polishing will not predictably darken shade.
n.0: Re-etching does not address colour assessment.

10.q: A nurse is explaining to a patient how gum disease develops. What is the correct sequence of periodontal disease progression?
10.w: Disease progresses from health to gingivitis and then to periodontitis if untreated.

n.3: This reverses the correct progression.
n.0: Health does not follow gingivitis without intervention.
n.2: Periodontitis does not precede gingivitis.
n.4: This sequence is incorrect.

10.q: Addition silicone impressions can often be poured later than alginate impressions. Which material property best explains this?
10.w: Addition silicone has good dimensional stability, allowing more flexibility before casting models.

n.3: Radiopacity is not the reason an impression can be poured later.
n.1: Electrical conductivity is irrelevant in this context.
n.2: High thermal expansion would reduce accuracy rather than improve storage time.
n.4: Surface roughness does not primarily determine delayed pouring suitability.

10.q: Which feature in the image most strongly indicates tongue-position error rather than movement?
o: A defined radiolucent band above the maxillary teeth
Generalised loss of sharpness across the whole image
Uneven density on one side only
10.w: A clear dark band above the maxillary teeth is the classic sign of failure to place the tongue to the palate.

n.3: Generalised blur is more typical of movement.
n.2: Double outlines suggest movement rather than tongue position.
n.4: Unilateral density change is not the key sign here.
n.1: Blurred condyles indicate movement or positioning issues.

10.q: A conscious diabetic patient is shaky, confused and sweating. They are able to swallow safely. What is the best action?
o: Give fast-acting glucose and reassess response
Give GTN spray under the tongue
Place them in the recovery position immediately
Withhold all oral intake and continue observing
10.w: A conscious patient with likely hypoglycaemia who can swallow should receive fast-acting glucose promptly.

n.2: Recovery position is for an unconscious breathing patient.
n.1: GTN is used for angina, not low blood glucose.
n.4: Delaying treatment may worsen hypoglycaemia.
n.3: CPR is not indicated in a conscious responsive patient.

10.q: Using the image, identify item number 1 most accurately.
10.w: Item 1 shows a tray arranged with surgical instruments and materials.

n.1: Debond kits contain orthodontic items.
n.4: Whitening kits are different.
n.0: Denture repair items are not shown.
n.2: A chart folder is not an instrument tray.

10.q: Full waste bags are being taken from the surgery to the external store. Which action best reduces risk when moving waste bags internally?
o: Carrying several bags in one hand
Throwing bags into the store room
Using a designated trolley or safe handling method
10.w: Using suitable transport methods reduces manual handling injury and contamination risk.

n.1: Dragging bags may split them.
n.2: Holding waste against clothing risks contamination.
n.3: Throwing bags may rupture them.
n.0: Overloading one hand is unsafe.

10.q: Interpret the deposits seen in the image.
10.w: Calculus is mineralised plaque adhering to tooth surfaces.

n.2: Food debris is not hardened or attached like this.
n.1: Caries involves demineralisation, not deposits.
n.4: Staining does not form hardened deposits.
n.3: No restorative material is present.

10.q: Which interpretation best explains the increased severity seen in the final stage of the image?
o: Chronic inflammation leading to tissue destruction
10.w: Chronic inflammation from plaque leads to destruction of periodontal tissues in advanced disease.

n.2: Improved hygiene would reduce severity.
n.4: Reduced plaque would not lead to progression.
n.3: Fluoride does not cause periodontal destruction.
n.1: Enamel strength is not relevant here.

10.q: Amalgam is being placed into a deep occlusal cavity in a lower molar. Which instrument type is most suitable for compacting amalgam firmly into a cavity preparation to reduce voids?
10.w: A condenser is used to compact amalgam into the cavity and improve adaptation.

n.1: A carver is used later to shape and refine occlusal anatomy.
n.0: An applicator brush is used for applying some liquids or resins, not condensing amalgam.
n.4: A matrix band is a supporting device for wall formation, not a condensing instrument.
n.3: A dappen dish is a container, not a hand instrument.

10.q: A pouch indicator strip has not changed to the expected colour after sterilisation. What should this be interpreted as?
10.w: Failure of the indicator to change suggests the process may not have met required conditions and the item should be investigated/reprocessed.

n.3: Indicator failure does not confirm sterility.
n.1: A passed cycle cannot be assumed from a failed indicator.
n.0: Chemical indicators are part of process monitoring.
n.4: Being unopened does not compensate for a failed process indicator.

10.q: A pouch falls onto a clean worktop while being unloaded and remains sealed. What is the best action?
10.w: If the pouch remains intact and the surface is clean, package integrity should be checked before deciding release.

n.1: Automatic disposal may be unnecessary if integrity is maintained.
n.2: Opening breaks the sterile barrier.
n.4: Washing the pouch is not appropriate.
n.3: Immediate use without checks is poor practice.

10.q: Using the image, what is the most likely cause of the rough ledge retaining plaque?
10.w: Overhanging restorations trap plaque and contribute to periodontal inflammation.

n.4: A sound contour would not create a ledge.
n.1: Normal anatomy does not form an artificial overhang.
n.3: Polished surfaces are smoother, not plaque retentive.
n.0: A clean margin should not appear as a rough ledge.

10.q: A team is reviewing incidents from the previous month. Which option best identifies a sharps near miss?
o: Scalpel falls to floor but injures nobody
10.w: An event that could have caused injury but did not is a near miss.

n.2: Correct disposal is not a near miss.
n.0: Routine replacement is not a near miss.
n.1: Glove changing is routine infection control.
n.4: Tray wiping is routine cleaning.

10.q: A parent attends with a child for treatment. What should be recognised about consent?
o: Consent depends on age, capacity and legal authority under local rules
The accompanying parent can always consent for any child
The child can consent alone from the age of sixteen only
The dentist decides whether consent is needed in each case
Written consent from both parents is always required
10.w: Consent for children depends on the child's competence, age and who has authority to consent.

n.1: Only someone with parental responsibility can consent, which not every accompanying adult has.
n.2: A younger child with sufficient understanding may be able to consent.
n.3: Consent is always required; the question is who can give it.
n.4: One person with parental responsibility is generally sufficient.

10.q: Using the image, identify item number 1.
10.w: Item 1 shows materials and items associated with prosthetic procedures.

n.1: Minor surgery trays contain different instruments.
n.0: Endodontic kits contain canal instruments.
n.3: Chart packs are not tray setups like this.
n.2: Bonding sets contain orthodontic items.

10.q: A patient with a history of angina develops central chest pressure during treatment that improves after using their GTN spray. Which condition is most likely recognised?
10.w: Chest discomfort relieved by GTN in a patient with known angina is consistent with an angina episode.

n.0: Cardiac arrest presents with collapse and absent normal responsiveness.
n.2: Hypoglycaemia usually causes sweating, confusion or behavioural change.
n.1: Seizure presents differently with abnormal movements or altered awareness.
n.4: Stroke commonly causes focal neurological deficits rather than GTN-responsive chest pain.

10.q: Based on the image, what is the most appropriate interpretation of the lesion observed on the tongue?
o: A suspicious lesion requiring urgent referral
A traumatic ulcer likely to heal within days
10.w: A non-healing, irregular ulcer with indurated appearance is suspicious and requires urgent referral for further investigation.

n.4: Traumatic ulcers typically resolve within 7–14 days and appear less irregular.
n.0: Fibrous growths do not present as ulcerated lesions.
n.2: This is not a normal anatomical feature.
n.1: Fungal infections usually present as removable white patches rather than ulceration.

10.q: A tray of contaminated instruments is placed on the clean packing bench because the dirty bench is full. What is the best action?
10.w: Contaminated instruments should be moved immediately to the designated dirty area to maintain workflow segregation.

n.1: Even short placement risks contaminating the clean bench.
n.0: Covering does not correct the zoning breach.
n.3: Packing around contaminated items is unsafe.
n.4: Delay does not address the immediate risk.

10.q: A patient with reduced manual dexterity struggles to brush effectively. What is the best recommendation?
o: Brush less often to reduce frustration
Consider a powered toothbrush with a small head
Use a larger hard manual brush
Use only floss instead of brushing
10.w: Powered brushes can improve plaque removal for patients with limited dexterity and may be easier to handle.

n.3: A hard larger brush may be harder to control and may cause trauma.
n.0: Reducing brushing frequency worsens plaque control.
n.4: Floss does not replace toothbrushing.
n.2: Changing toothpaste does not solve brushing difficulty.

10.q: After a temporary restoration is placed, the patient says the tooth feels high when biting together. What is the best action?
o: Advise the patient to avoid chewing on that side for several days
Ask the operator to assess the occlusion before the patient leaves
Explain that all temporary restorations feel high at first and dismiss the patient
Offer analgesics because post-operative tenderness is expected
Suggest that the patient wait until the anaesthetic wears off before deciding
10.w: A restoration that feels high should be assessed by the operator before the patient leaves, as it may require occlusal adjustment.

n.2: A high restoration should not simply be dismissed as normal because it may cause pain or damage.
n.0: Chewing advice does not correct an occlusal discrepancy if one is present.
n.4: Anaesthetic can alter sensation, but a reported high bite still requires assessment.
n.3: Analgesics do not address the possible mechanical cause of the patient's complaint.

10.q: A patient reports sensitivity to cold two days after a deep restoration. Which explanation is most appropriate to relay to the operator?
o: It always means the tooth requires extraction
It can be ignored for several months
It is caused only by local anaesthetic
Post-operative sensitivity may need assessment of occlusion, depth or seal
10.w: Post-operative sensitivity can have several causes and should be clinically assessed.

n.4: Sensitivity alone does not prove failure.
n.0: Extraction is not automatically indicated.
n.2: Local anaesthetic is not the sole explanation days later.
n.1: Persistent symptoms should not be ignored.

10.q: A repeat radiograph is required after obtaining an image similar to this one. What is the best action before retaking it?
o: Ask the patient to bite harder only
Reduce vertical angulation and reposition the receptor parallel to the tooth
10.w: Foreshortening is corrected by reducing excessive vertical angulation and improving receptor alignment.

n.1: Exposure time changes density, not image distortion.
n.3: Mesial tubehead rotation changes horizontal angulation rather than correcting foreshortening.
n.4: Receptor size alone will not correct the angulation error.
n.0: Patient bite pressure alone does not resolve projection geometry errors.

10.q: A patient is breathing rapidly, has tingling fingers, dizziness and appears very anxious after treatment starts. What is the most likely emergency being recognised?
10.w: Rapid breathing with tingling and anxiety is consistent with hyperventilation.

n.4: Stroke more commonly causes focal neurological deficits.
n.3: Hypoglycaemia commonly causes sweating and confusion rather than tingling from overbreathing.
n.1: Anaphylaxis usually involves allergic signs such as rash or wheeze.
n.0: Airway obstruction would impair airflow rather than cause overbreathing.

10.q: A student asks how a small lesion becomes a painful tooth. Which sequence correctly describes caries progression?
10.w: Caries progresses from enamel to dentine and then to pulp.

n.0: Caries starts in enamel.
n.4: Pulp is affected last.
n.3: Pulp is not affected before dentine.
n.1: Enamel is always first.

10.q: A dental nurse is asked to assist in examining a duct opening located opposite the upper second molar. Which gland does this duct belong to?
10.w: The parotid duct (Stensen’s duct) opens opposite the upper second molar.

n.4: The submandibular duct opens under the tongue.
n.3: The sublingual gland has multiple small ducts under the tongue.
n.1: Palatal glands are minor glands without this duct location.
n.0: Buccal glands are minor glands and do not have a major duct opening here.

10.q: During cementation of an indirect restoration, moisture repeatedly contaminates the tooth. What is the most likely consequence if uncontrolled?
10.w: Many luting agents are sensitive to contamination, which may reduce retention and marginal seal.

n.3: Moisture generally harms rather than improves retention.
n.0: Shade is unrelated.
n.2: Anaesthetic onset is unrelated.
n.4: Occlusion still requires checking.

10.q: A patient wearing fixed orthodontic appliances reports bleeding gums around brackets. Which oral hygiene advice is best?
o: Advise a soft brush used once daily to reduce irritation
Demonstrate brushing carefully around brackets and advise use of interdental aids
Recommend chlorhexidine mouthwash in place of brushing
Suggest a single-tufted brush around brackets only
Wait until the appliance is removed before resuming normal brushing
10.w: Plaque retention around brackets is common; targeted brushing and interdental cleaning help reduce inflammation.

n.0: Reducing frequency allows more plaque to accumulate, worsening the bleeding.
n.2: A useful adjunct for a short period, but it does not remove plaque mechanically.
n.3: Helpful around brackets, but leaves interdental areas uncleaned.
n.4: Bleeding is a sign of inflammation from plaque; stopping cleaning makes it worse.

10.q: Based on the image, which periodontal finding is most clearly demonstrated around the lower incisors?
o: Gingival recession with root surface exposure
10.w: The image shows apical migration of the gingival margin with visible root surface exposure, which is consistent with gingival recession.

n.3: Gingival hyperplasia presents as enlarged gingival tissues rather than recession and exposed root surfaces.
n.0: Pericoronitis is associated with partially erupted teeth, most commonly third molars.
n.1: Attrition affects the incisal or occlusal surfaces, not the gingival margin.
n.2: Denture-induced stomatitis affects the mucosa beneath a denture, not the gingiva around natural teeth.

10.q: A team member removes eye protection by touching the front surface after treatment. What is the likely risk?
o: Self-contamination from the contaminated outer surface
10.w: The front of eye protection may be contaminated and should be handled by straps or sides where possible.

n.1: Grip is not the safety priority.
n.3: Fogging is unrelated to removal technique.
n.0: The main issue is contamination, not glove damage.
n.2: Apron coverage is unrelated.

11.q: An anterior composite is being built up in several layers rather than placed in one piece. A composite restoration is placed in small increments rather than one bulk mass to help control which material property effect?
11.w: Incremental placement helps reduce stresses associated with polymerisation shrinkage and improves curing depth.

n.2: Radiopacity is determined by formulation, not increment size.
n.3: Tea staining is not the main reason for incremental placement.
n.4: Taste alteration is unrelated.
n.0: Magnetic attraction is irrelevant.

11.q: The image shows progression toward the pulp. What protective response may occur?
11.w: Secondary dentine forms as a defence mechanism to protect the pulp.

n.2: Plaque increases risk, not protection.
n.3: Reduced saliva increases risk.
n.0: Enamel does not thicken in response.
n.1: Gum recession is unrelated.

11.q: A nurse is working at the clean bench after a processing run. Which bench activity is most appropriate in the clean zone?
11.w: Checking processed sealed packs for storage is a clean-zone activity.

n.2: Dirty tray receipt belongs in the dirty zone.
n.3: Rinsing contaminated items is a dirty-zone task.
n.4: Waste sorting should be segregated from clean areas.
n.1: Manual cleaning of used burs is a dirty-zone task.

11.q: A six-point pocket chart is being recorded for a patient with poor plaque control. Which finding most strongly indicates gingival inflammation during assessment?
11.w: Bleeding on probing is a common sign of inflamed gingival tissues.

n.3: Absence of plaque does not indicate inflammation.
n.1: Dry stippled gingivae are usually healthier findings.
n.2: Occlusal enamel status is unrelated.
n.4: Margins alone do not confirm gingivitis.

11.q: During CPR, chest compressions are being delivered too slowly at around 60 per minute. Which interpretation is most accurate?
o: The rate is acceptable when two rescuers are present
The rate is ideal if compressions are deeper
The rate is inadequate and should be increased
The rate only matters once the AED arrives
The rate should be reduced further to avoid fatigue
11.w: An adult compression rate of about 100–120 per minute is recommended, so 60 per minute is too slow.

n.1: Depth does not compensate for an inadequate compression rate.
n.0: Two rescuers do not change the target compression rate.
n.4: Reducing the rate further would worsen perfusion.
n.3: Effective compressions matter immediately, not only after AED arrival.

11.q: A patient who smokes twenty cigarettes a day attends with deepening pockets. What is the most appropriate action for a dental nurse when managing a patient with smoking-related periodontal risk?
o: Focus on scaling and leave lifestyle advice to the dentist
Provide smoking cessation advice and oral hygiene instruction
Recommend a high-fluoride toothpaste and review
Record smoking status and raise it at the next recall
Warn the patient that treatment may not work while they smoke
11.w: Smoking cessation advice combined with oral hygiene instruction is key in managing periodontal risk.

n.0: Prevention advice is squarely within the dental nurse's role.
n.2: Targets caries risk rather than the periodontal risk from smoking.
n.3: Recording is right, but the opportunity to advise is now.
n.4: True but discouraging; brief cessation advice is more effective than a warning.

11.q: An audit of the sharps containers is carried out across the practice. Which action is an example of poor sharps segregation?
o: Placing a used blade in sharps waste
Placing paper packaging in sharps waste routinely
11.w: Non-sharp waste should not routinely occupy sharps containers.

n.1: Blades belong in sharps disposal.
n.0: Closing full bins is appropriate.
n.4: Correct container use is good practice.
n.3: Damaged bins should be reported.

11.q: After removing an alginate impression, the nurse sees many small bubbles on the occlusal surfaces. What is the most likely error?
o: Air incorporated while loading the tray
The impression was rinsed after removal
Water was too cold during mixing
11.w: Air trapped during loading often creates surface voids and bubbles.

n.3: Tray rigidity is not the common cause of surface bubbles.
n.4: Cold water slows set rather than causing bubbles directly.
n.1: Rinsing is appropriate and not the main cause.
n.2: Light closure does not usually produce multiple bubbles.

11.q: Heavy deposits are noted on the lingual surfaces of the lower incisors. Which best action is most appropriate after identifying localised heavy calculus around the lower anterior teeth?
o: Advise the patient to avoid cleaning that area
Arrange periodontal treatment and reinforce effective plaque control measures
11.w: The correct next step is periodontal management through professional treatment and reinforcement of effective plaque control.

n.0: Avoiding cleaning would increase plaque accumulation and worsen inflammation.
n.2: A dressing does not remove the underlying plaque-retentive calculus.
n.3: Antifungal medication is not indicated for calculus-associated periodontal disease.
n.4: Endodontic therapy treats pulpal disease, not routine periodontal calculus accumulation.

11.q: A team member posts about an unusual case they saw at work that day. Why should staff avoid discussing patients on social media, even without naming them?
o: Details may still identify the patient or breach trust
It is acceptable if done after work
11.w: Seemingly anonymous details can still identify individuals and undermine confidentiality.

n.3: Internet speed is irrelevant.
n.1: Patient confidentiality is not marketing content.
n.4: Social media does not replace records.
n.2: Professional duties continue outside work.

11.q: A sterilised pouch is placed beside a container of used burs. What is the main concern?
11.w: Placing clean stock beside contaminated items compromises clean and dirty zone separation.

n.0: Label fading is not the primary concern.
n.4: The issue is contamination control, not stock levels.
n.2: Instrument sharpness is unrelated.
n.3: Workflow speed is secondary.

11.q: A patient attends for a planned surgical procedure. What is the main reason for checking medical history before oral surgery?
11.w: Medical history may reveal conditions or medicines affecting surgery and healing.

n.0: Shade selection is unrelated.
n.4: Denture tooth selection is unrelated.
n.1: Arch size is not the main reason.
n.3: Time reduction is not the clinical purpose.

11.q: A patient attends with facial swelling and severe pain. Which of the following actions is inappropriate when assisting with a patient with a suspected dental abscess?
11.w: Delaying treatment risks spread of infection and complications.

n.4: Recording is appropriate.
n.0: Alerting the dentist is essential.
n.3: Reassurance is appropriate.
n.2: Preparation is appropriate.

11.q: A broken glass medicine ampoule is discarded into general waste. What is the best action?
11.w: Broken glass capable of causing injury should be placed in the appropriate sharps container or approved stream.

n.1: Wrapping does not remove sharps risk.
n.4: Pushing it deeper is unsafe.
n.3: Storage does not control the hazard.
n.0: Covering it with paper is unsafe.

11.q: Space is limited and clean packs are placed above the dirty sink. What is the main issue?
11.w: Storage above a dirty sink exposes clean packs to splash and aerosol contamination risk.

n.4: Height is secondary to contamination risk.
n.0: Readability is not the primary concern.
n.1: Walking distance is less important than hygiene.
n.2: Appearance is irrelevant.

11.q: A patient with long-standing gingivitis now shows early attachment loss. Which factor most strongly contributes to the progression from gingivitis to periodontitis?
11.w: Persistent plaque accumulation leads to chronic inflammation and progression to periodontitis.

n.1: Fluoride does not cause periodontal disease.
n.2: Low sugar intake does not promote progression.
n.4: Regular visits reduce progression risk.
n.0: Frequent brushing helps prevent disease.

11.q: A practice is reviewing the chemicals used in the decontamination room. Why are COSHH assessments important in dental practice?
o: They are only for large hospitals
They identify hazards and control exposure to substances
They remove the need for PPE
11.w: COSHH assessments help identify hazardous substances and specify controls to reduce exposure risk.

n.4: Induction and training are still required.
n.3: PPE may still be necessary.
n.0: COSHH applies across many workplaces including dental practices.
n.1: No system can guarantee zero accidents.

11.q: An adult in cardiac arrest has just been defibrillated. After a shock is delivered, what sequence should follow next?
o: Check for a pulse and breathing before continuing
Remove the pads and reassess the airway
Resume CPR immediately and follow further AED prompts
Wait for the AED to confirm the rhythm has changed
Watch for signs of life for thirty seconds before restarting
11.w: CPR should restart immediately after a shock unless the patient shows clear signs of recovery, following AED prompts.

n.0: A return of circulation is uncommon immediately after a shock, and checking wastes compression time.
n.1: Pads stay on so the AED can re-analyse.
n.3: The AED will re-analyse after two minutes; compressions continue meanwhile.
n.4: Half a minute without compressions after a shock is a significant loss.

11.q: On the image, item 6 would most commonly contain which restorative adjunct?
11.w: Small opaque dropper bottles commonly contain bonding agents or primers.

n.0: Alginate powder is stored in tubs or sachets.
n.1: Amalgam alloy is supplied in capsules.
n.4: Zinc phosphate powder is jar supplied.
n.3: Putty silicone is supplied in tubs or cartridges.

11.q: The dentist reports recurrent voids in a mixed alginate impression. Which error is most likely?
11.w: Poor spatulation commonly traps air and leaves voids in alginate.

n.4: Water temperature mainly alters setting time.
n.1: A clean damp tray is not the primary cause of voids.
n.2: Perforated trays help retention rather than cause voids.
n.3: Closed storage is desirable.

11.q: Interpret the dark staining and deposits seen in the image.
11.w: The deposits represent calculus with plaque accumulation.

n.2: Staining alone is not hardened like calculus.
n.1: Caries appears as demineralisation, not deposits.
n.4: No restorative material is present.
n.3: Fluorosis affects enamel appearance.

11.q: A patient attends for a full assessment of their gums. What should the dental nurse prepare before periodontal charting begins?
11.w: A periodontal probe is essential for recording pocket depths and bleeding points.

n.4: Shade tabs are used for restorative shade matching.
n.0: Impression materials are unnecessary for charting.
n.3: Rubber dam equipment is unrelated.
n.1: Crown removal instruments are not required.

11.q: An audit finds domestic waste being placed into clinical waste bags. What is the main risk of mixing domestic and clinical waste unnecessarily?
o: Higher disposal cost and poor compliance
11.w: Incorrectly classifying waste can increase costs and breach disposal requirements.

n.1: Colour is irrelevant.
n.3: Collections are not improved by poor segregation.
n.0: Storage is not the main issue.
n.2: Floor cleanliness is unrelated.

11.q: A patient begins to struggle for breath partway through a meal in the waiting area. Which feature best identifies airway obstruction in a conscious adult patient?
o: Unable to speak or cough effectively
Warm flushed skin with no distress
11.w: Inability to speak or cough effectively suggests severe airway obstruction.

n.0: Toothache alone does not indicate choking.
n.4: No distress signs make airway obstruction unlikely.
n.2: Speaking normally suggests airway patency.
n.1: Headache alone does not indicate obstruction.

11.q: An occlusal cavity in an upper premolar is ready to receive amalgam. Which instrument is specifically used to pack amalgam into a cavity preparation?
11.w: A condenser is designed to compact amalgam and reduce voids.

n.0: A burnisher smooths and contours surfaces.
n.2: An excavator removes soft material or debris.
n.3: A probe is for examination.
n.4: A scaler removes deposits.

11.q: A bitewing radiograph shows the crowns of the upper and lower posterior teeth, but the interproximal contacts are heavily overlapped as seen in the image. What is the most likely cause of this error?
11.w: Overlapped interproximal contacts are most commonly caused by incorrect horizontal angulation, where the beam is not directed through the contact points.

n.0: Vertical angulation errors usually distort crown and root length rather than causing contact overlap.
n.1: A reversed film packet produces a herringbone or tyre-track appearance, not contact overlap.
n.4: Underexposure creates a pale image but does not specifically overlap contacts.
n.3: Movement causes blurring or loss of sharpness rather than consistent overlap of contacts.

11.q: A patient asks how they should look after their new denture at home. Which advice is most appropriate for cleaning dentures?
11.w: A suitable brush and gentle cleaning help maintain the denture safely.

n.2: Wire brushes may damage surfaces.
n.3: Boiling bleach is inappropriate and damaging.
n.1: Leaving dentures uncleaned encourages deposits.
n.0: Filing stains damages the appliance.

11.q: A new team member is unsure where an item of waste belongs. What is the safest response if you are unsure which bin an item belongs in?
o: Ask a trained colleague or check local policy
11.w: If uncertain, consult guidance or trained staff rather than guessing.

n.1: Guessing can lead to incorrect segregation.
n.3: Domestic waste may be inappropriate.
n.2: Storage in drawers is unsafe.
n.4: Practice waste should not be taken home.

11.q: A dental nurse is explaining tooth structure to a student on placement. Which sequence correctly describes the layers from the outer crown to the centre of the tooth?
11.w: The correct sequence is enamel (outer), dentine (middle), and pulp (centre).

n.1: Dentine is not outermost.
n.4: Pulp is central, not outer.
n.3: Pulp is not between enamel and dentine.
n.0: Cementum is not part of the crown.

11.q: A restorative material is chosen for an anterior tooth because it closely mimics natural enamel appearance. Which property is most relevant?
11.w: Aesthetic translucency helps a material blend with natural enamel and dentine appearance.

n.1: Electrical conductivity is unrelated to appearance.
n.4: Odour is not an aesthetic matching property.
n.2: Maximum opacity alone may make the result appear artificial.
n.3: Dissolution rate would be undesirable clinically.

11.q: A practice is planning the layout of a new decontamination room. Which item should be positioned nearest the washing stage?
11.w: Used instruments should enter directly into the dirty receiving/cleaning stage of the workflow.

n.2: Sterile stock should be kept in clean areas away from dirty workflow.
n.1: Patient records are unrelated.
n.3: Refreshments should not be in decontamination workflow areas.
n.0: Clean handpieces belong in a clean storage area.

11.q: A patient is leaving the practice with their new dentures fitted. Which postoperative advice is most appropriate after receiving a new denture?
11.w: Review visits allow safe adjustments and monitoring of adaptation.

n.0: Patients should not bend clasps themselves.
n.4: Boiling water may distort the denture.
n.3: Continuous wear is not always advised.
n.2: Self-filing may damage fit and tissues.

11.q: A child is at increased caries risk. Which action is most appropriate regarding fluoride products?
11.w: Higher-risk children may need tailored advice on fluoride strength from a dental professional.

n.3: Adult products may be unsuitable without guidance.
n.2: Stopping fluoride removes a protective measure.
n.4: Whitening products do not replace risk-based fluoride advice.
n.0: Brushing without toothpaste loses fluoride benefit.

11.q: An unfamiliar item is found on a tray with no wrapper or label. Which is the safest response if you are unsure whether an item is contaminated and sharp?
o: Ask a colleague to identify it before anyone touches it
Assume it is clean if it looks visibly clean
Handle it as a sharp until assessed
Place it straight into the washer-disinfector to make it safe
Set it aside on the worktop until the end of the session
11.w: When uncertain, using a cautious sharps approach reduces injury risk.

n.0: Sensible, but it transfers the risk rather than controlling it.
n.1: Contamination is not reliably visible.
n.3: Loading an unidentified sharp by hand is the risky step.
n.4: Leaves an unidentified sharp where someone else may meet it.

11.q: A nurse discusses a patient's treatment loudly in the waiting room. What is the main concern?
11.w: Discussing patient information where others can hear may breach confidentiality.

n.4: Crowding is secondary to the privacy issue.
n.1: Timing is not the key concern.
n.3: Speaking clearly is not the issue.
n.2: Chair occupancy is irrelevant.

11.q: A nurse is preparing for a procedure where blood spatter is likely. Which item of PPE is primarily intended to protect clothing and exposed skin from splashes?
11.w: Disposable aprons protect clothing and torso areas from contamination.

n.3: Masks protect the respiratory area.
n.4: Goggles protect eyes.
n.1: Gloves protect hands.
n.2: Hair clips are not PPE for splash protection.

11.q: The waste contractor collects from the practice each month. Why should waste collections be documented where required?
o: To provide records of lawful transfer and disposal
11.w: Transfer records support legal compliance and traceability of waste movements.

n.1: Documentation is not for decoration.
n.4: Records do not affect bag strength.
n.2: Training is still required.
n.0: Cleaning schedules are separate.

11.q: Several lower molar periapicals in one session show the same missing-apex appearance as this image. What is the most likely cause?
o: Exposure time is consistently too long
The processor temperature is too low
The receptor is repeatedly positioned too coronally
11.w: Repeated loss of apices usually means the receptor is consistently being placed too high, failing to cover the root ends.

n.0: Long exposure affects density rather than image coverage.
n.2: Swallowing may cause blur, not consistent apical cut-off.
n.3: Low processor temperature affects development, not receptor position.
n.1: Horizontal angulation affects contacts more than apical inclusion.

11.q: Which surface of a maxillary incisor faces the palate?
11.w: The lingual surface of maxillary incisors faces the palate.

n.1: Labial surfaces face the lips.
n.0: Buccal surfaces apply to posterior teeth.
n.4: Occlusal surfaces are not present on incisors.
n.3: Mesial surfaces are toward the midline.

11.q: A patient who has not attended for three years presents with widespread hard deposits. What is the most appropriate action for a dental nurse when identifying heavy calculus deposits in a patient?
o: Apply fluoride varnish and review at the next recall
Polish the deposits to improve the appearance
Provide dietary advice and rebook in twelve months
Provide oral hygiene instruction and refer for scaling
Recommend a tartar-control toothpaste and monitor
11.w: Oral hygiene instruction and referral for professional scaling are essential in managing calculus-related periodontal risk.

n.0: Addresses caries risk but leaves the calculus untouched.
n.1: Polishing over calculus leaves the deposit and the plaque beneath it.
n.2: Diet has little bearing on calculus, and a year is too long.
n.4: May slow new deposits but cannot remove established calculus.

11.q: Identify the gingival condition in the image.
11.w: The gingiva appear red, swollen, and bleeding, indicating inflammation.

n.0: Fibrotic gingiva would appear firm and pale.
n.1: Healthy gingiva are not red or bleeding.
n.4: No ulceration or necrosis is visible.
n.2: Hyperplasia involves enlargement rather than inflammation.

11.q: A patient returns a week after receiving new complete dentures. Which patient complaint most suggests the bite may need adjustment on new dentures?
11.w: Uneven contacts may indicate occlusal discrepancies needing adjustment.

n.1: Colour alone does not indicate bite issues.
n.0: Box labelling is unrelated.
n.4: Storage cup moisture is unrelated.
n.2: A smooth flange does not suggest occlusal problems.

11.q: A dental nurse notices a chart incorrectly stating that enamel contains living cells. What is the error?
11.w: Enamel is non-vital and does not contain living cells.

n.3: Enamel is not vascular.
n.1: Enamel does not contain nerves.
n.0: Enamel does not contain collagen.
n.4: Enamel cannot regenerate.

11.q: A patient is being reviewed following a course of periodontal treatment. Which record is most useful when monitoring periodontal treatment over time?
11.w: Pocket charting provides measurable data for comparison over time.

n.0: Bite registration records occlusion.
n.4: Shade maps are restorative records.
n.1: Cast trimming notes are unrelated.
n.2: A lab docket does not monitor periodontal status.

11.q: A wax denture has been returned from the laboratory for the next stage. What is the main purpose of a try-in appointment for complete dentures?
11.w: Try-in appointments allow checks of appearance, occlusion and basic fit before completion.

n.4: Radiographs are not the main purpose.
n.3: Calculus removal is periodontal treatment.
n.2: Pocket depths are periodontal measurements.
n.1: Extraction is unrelated.

11.q: A nurse notices confidential patient paperwork in a domestic bin. What should be recognised as the main issue?
o: Incorrect segregation of clinical and domestic waste
Insufficient waste bins provided in the area
Records being removed from the practice management system
Staff not following the practice's recycling policy
11.w: Patient-identifiable information must be disposed of securely to maintain confidentiality.

n.1: Paperwork is not clinical waste; the issue is confidentiality, not the stream.
n.2: May be a contributing factor, but it is not the main issue.
n.3: Nothing here suggests the electronic record was altered.
n.4: Recycling is not the concern with identifiable patient data.

11.q: A periapical radiograph of the lower posterior region shows the distal aspect of the most posterior molar cut off at the image edge. What is the most likely interpretation of this fault?
o: The image is overexposed and distal enamel has been burned out
The patient moved during exposure causing loss of the distal crown
The receptor was positioned too far mesially, resulting in incomplete coverage of the posterior tooth
The roots are shortened due to excessive vertical angulation
The x-ray beam was underpowered and failed to penetrate the molar
11.w: When the distal surface of the terminal tooth is cut off, the receptor is commonly positioned too far forwards, so posterior anatomy is excluded.

n.0: Overexposure affects density across the image rather than removing one side of a tooth.
n.1: Movement causes blur or double outlines, not clean loss at the image edge.
n.4: Low exposure reduces density but does not selectively remove distal anatomy.
n.3: Vertical angulation changes tooth length, not posterior coverage.

11.q: A dental nurse notices a patient consistently misses cleaning the surfaces facing the tongue. What advice should be given?
o: Advise using a mouthwash after brushing
Increase brushing time on the buccal surfaces
Recommend an interdental brush for the front teeth
Suggest a whitening toothpaste for better coverage
11.w: Lingual surfaces face the tongue and require effective brushing.

n.0: A useful adjunct, but it does not remove plaque from surfaces the brush is missing.
n.2: Spends more effort on the surfaces already being cleaned well.
n.3: Cleans between teeth rather than the tongue-facing surfaces being missed.
n.4: Toothpaste choice does not change which surfaces the brush reaches.

11.q: After curing a composite increment, the surface remains tacky. What is the best interpretation?
11.w: A superficial tacky oxygen-inhibited layer is expected and aids bonding between increments.

n.0: Composite does not melt in this context.
n.1: Etchant strength does not create this classic surface finding.
n.2: Matrix tension is unrelated.
n.4: Shade guide contamination is irrelevant.

11.q: Instruments have completed processing and are being put away. Which item should move last into the clean zone?
11.w: Processed sealed packs are the final clean output entering the clean zone.

n.4: Used burs are contaminated.
n.0: Waste should never move into the clean zone.
n.3: Soiled liners are waste.
n.1: Dirty handles require processing first.

11.q: A dental nurse is assisting during examination of a tooth with visible cavitation. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Apply a desensitising agent to the exposed surface
Chart the tooth as sound and review at recall
Provide dietary advice and arrange a routine recall
Record findings and prepare for restoration
Take an impression in case a crown is needed
11.w: Recording and assisting with restorative preparation is appropriate.

n.0: Treats a symptom while leaving the cavity untreated.
n.1: An inaccurate record that hides visible cavitation.
n.2: Important prevention, but the cavity still needs restoring now.
n.4: Anticipates treatment the dentist has not planned.

11.q: A patient attends with a non-healing ulcer of six weeks' duration. Which of the following represents an error in managing a patient with suspected oral cancer?
11.w: Providing reassurance without referral is inappropriate when malignancy is suspected and delays diagnosis.

n.0: Documentation is essential for monitoring and referral.
n.3: Urgent referral is correct management.
n.4: A full history is necessary.
n.2: Recording risk factors is good clinical practice.

11.q: A radiopaque object is visible in the floor of the mouth region on the image shown. What is the best action for the clinician?
o: Arrange extraction of the nearest tooth as the likely source
Correlate clinically and consider further assessment for a salivary calculus
Record it as a normal mandibular anatomical landmark
Repeat the radiograph with a longer exposure to clarify
Report it as a retained root fragment in the records
11.w: A discrete radiopaque body in the floor of the mouth region may represent a salivary calculus and should be correlated with symptoms and examined further.

n.0: Acts on an assumption before the finding has been assessed.
n.2: Dismissing an unexpected opacity as anatomy risks missing pathology.
n.3: An additional exposure without clinical justification is not acceptable.
n.4: Recording a diagnosis that has not been established.

11.q: A patient treated for hypoglycaemia becomes alert and symptoms resolve. What is the best next step?
o: Give GTN spray to prevent relapse
Lay the patient flat for one hour regardless of condition
Monitor, provide longer-acting carbohydrate if appropriate, and reassess
Send the patient home alone at once
11.w: After recovery, continued monitoring and follow-up carbohydrate intake may help maintain glucose levels.

n.3: Immediate treatment restart may be inappropriate.
n.4: Abrupt discharge without reassessment may be unsafe.
n.0: GTN has no role in hypoglycaemia management.
n.1: Positioning should reflect the patient's condition, not a fixed rule.

11.q: A practice regularly runs late and appointments are compressed. Which behaviour most increases patient management problems in practice?
11.w: Rushing patients often leads to anxiety, confusion and dissatisfaction.

n.1: Clear explanations usually improve management.
n.0: Checking comfort supports positive care.
n.2: Listening helps address issues early.
n.3: Organisation reduces avoidable problems.

11.q: A patient with periodontal concerns asks where to focus cleaning first. What is the best action?
o: Clean only the areas that have stopped bleeding
Concentrate on the biting surfaces where food collects
Explain cleaning at the gum margin and between teeth is especially important
Focus on the tongue and palate first
11.w: Plaque commonly accumulates at the gingival margin and interdentally, so these areas need attention.

n.0: Bleeding sites are the inflamed ones and need cleaning most.
n.1: Relevant to caries risk, but periodontal disease starts at the gingival margin.
n.3: Helps with halitosis but does little for periodontal health.
n.4: Easy to reach and usually cleanest already; posterior and interdental sites are missed.

11.q: A nurse is explaining the decontamination process to a student. Which sequence best reflects correct movement of instruments through workflow?
11.w: Contaminated instruments are received, cleaned, sterilised and then stored ready for use.

n.3: Storage should not occur before cleaning.
n.2: Cleaning precedes sterilisation.
n.1: Storage should follow decontamination.
n.4: Packaging and use are in the wrong order.

11.q: Which anatomical or pathological feature is most appropriately assessed on the image shown?
o: Apical pathology of upper incisors only
Floor of mouth structures and localisation of radiopaque objects
11.w: Lower occlusal views are useful for assessing the mandibular arch, floor of mouth region and localising radiopaque objects such as calculi.

n.3: Upper premolar proximal caries are better assessed with bitewing radiographs.
n.1: TMJs are not shown on this occlusal image.
n.0: This is not the preferred image for isolated upper incisor apical assessment.
n.4: Soft tissue profile is assessed with cephalometric imaging.

11.q: A dental nurse is assisting during periodontal charting. The patient has bleeding on probing, recession and calculus deposits around the lower incisors. Which condition is most consistent with these findings?
o: Periodontitis affecting the lower anterior region
11.w: Bleeding on probing with recession and calculus in this context is most consistent with periodontitis affecting the lower anterior teeth.

n.4: Gingivitis alone does not account for the recession and periodontal support loss implied by the presentation.
n.2: A periapical abscess is related to pulpal infection and usually presents differently.
n.1: Oral candidosis affects mucosal tissues rather than causing calculus-associated periodontal destruction.
n.0: Irreversible pulpitis causes pulpal pain and is not diagnosed from gingival recession and calculus.

11.q: Equipment is being positioned in a newly fitted decontamination room. Which item should remain furthest from the clean storage area?
11.w: Used instrument receiving trays belong in the contaminated intake area, away from clean storage.

n.1: Labels may be used in clean areas.
n.3: Sealed pouches belong in clean storage.
n.0: Clean cassette racks should remain in clean areas.
n.4: Records may be kept in a clean admin area.

11.q: A manager inspects the clean zone during a routine audit. Which observation most strongly suggests a clean zone is being maintained correctly?
11.w: A clean zone containing only sealed processed packs indicates good segregation control.

n.3: Used trays should not be near the clean zone.
n.4: Waste bags do not belong in clean storage areas.
n.0: Dirty gloves indicate contamination.
n.2: Open exposed instruments lose protected status.

11.q: The panoramic radiograph shows a broad radiolucent band over the apices of the maxillary teeth. What is the most likely cause of this error?
o: Patient failed to place the tongue against the palate
11.w: A palatoglossal air space appears as a dark band over the maxillary apices when the tongue is not held against the palate during exposure.

n.3: Movement causes blurring or double outlines rather than a defined radiolucent band.
n.1: Lead apron artefact is usually radiopaque and lower in the image.
n.0: Short exposure reduces density but does not create this characteristic air space.
n.4: A reversed receptor would not create a horizontal dark band over the maxillary roots.

11.q: A repeat panoramic radiograph is required after obtaining an image similar to this one. What is the best action before retaking it?
o: Ensure the Frankfort plane is horizontal
Instruct the patient to press the tongue firmly against the palate throughout exposure
Position the incisors more anteriorly in the bite block
Straighten the spine and lower the shoulders
11.w: The correct preventive action is clear instruction for the patient to keep the tongue against the palate until the scan finishes.

n.0: Corrects a tilted occlusal plane, not a palatal air shadow.
n.2: Alters magnification of the anterior teeth rather than the palatal shadow.
n.3: Changes the curve of the occlusal plane and can introduce new errors.
n.4: Reduces the cervical spine shadow in the midline, a different artefact.

11.q: A patient with periodontal pockets is anxious about treatment noise. What is the best supportive action by the nurse?
11.w: Clear reassurance and explanation can reduce anxiety and improve cooperation.

n.4: Leaving the patient unsupported is inappropriate.
n.3: Extra noise may worsen anxiety.
n.0: Questions should be answered appropriately.
n.1: Unexpected treatment may increase distress.

11.q: A patient's denture has developed noticeable staining over several months. Which advice best helps prevent denture staining?
o: Rinse it under hot water after every meal
Soak it in a bleach-based solution weekly
Store it dry overnight to prevent staining
Use a whitening toothpaste on it daily
11.w: Regular appropriate cleaning helps reduce staining and plaque accumulation.

n.1: Rinsing helps a little, but hot water can distort the acrylic.
n.2: Bleach can damage the denture and is not recommended for routine cleaning.
n.3: Acrylic should be stored damp; drying can cause warping.
n.4: Whitening pastes are abrasive and scratch acrylic, which then stains more.

12.q: The image shows pus accumulation at the root apex. What is this composed of?
12.w: Pus consists of bacteria, dead tissue, and inflammatory cells.

n.4: Saliva is not involved in abscess formation.
n.2: Enamel proteins are not part of pus.
n.1: Pus is not composed of blood alone.
n.3: Fluoride does not form pus.

12.q: A patient is hesitating about proceeding with an extraction. Which behaviour most undermines voluntary consent?
o: Pressuring the patient by saying they have no choice
12.w: Consent must be freely given without coercion or undue pressure.

n.0: Questions support informed decisions.
n.4: Written information can support understanding.
n.1: Checking understanding is good practice.
n.2: Options help support choice.

12.q: A dental nurse notices swelling and redness near a decayed tooth. What is the correct action?
o: Advise the patient to rinse with warm salt water and review
Apply a topical antiseptic to the area
Note it in the record for the next appointment
Reassure the patient that swelling near decay is expected
Record findings and alert the dentist
12.w: The nurse must report findings to the dentist for diagnosis and management.

n.0: Sensible advice, but it does not replace assessment by the dentist.
n.1: Outside the nurse's scope for an undiagnosed swelling.
n.2: Recording is right; delaying the dentist's attention is not.
n.3: Offers a clinical opinion the nurse is not able to give.

12.q: A practice is reviewing its medical emergency preparedness after a near miss. Which management error regarding emergency drugs and equipment is most serious?
o: Not knowing where the emergency kit is stored
Training staff to locate the AED
12.w: If staff cannot locate the emergency kit quickly, critical treatment may be dangerously delayed.

n.0: Routine expiry checks are good practice.
n.3: Replacing used stock is appropriate and necessary.
n.1: Checklists support readiness rather than create risk.
n.4: Training staff to find the AED improves emergency response.

12.q: A stock tray is overloaded and excess impression material repeatedly causes gagging. What is the best action?
o: Choose a darker shade of impression material
Keep the tray in place longer before fully seating
Seat the tray more slowly to let the patient adapt
Select the correct tray and load an appropriate amount of material
Use the same tray but increase the amount to improve retention
12.w: Correct tray selection and appropriate loading reduce overflow, improve comfort and still allow adequate recording.

n.4: Increasing the amount would likely worsen overflow and gagging.
n.2: Slower seating does not solve overloading.
n.1: Delaying seating is unlikely to improve the situation and may affect accuracy.
n.0: Shade is irrelevant to impression tray loading.

12.q: Cleaning chemicals are being put away in the decontamination room. Which storage practice best supports COSHH compliance?
o: Decanted into clearly marked unbreakable containers
Kept in a locked cupboard with the labels removed for tidiness
Products stored in original labelled containers
Stored together by colour so staff can find them quickly
Stored with the safety data sheets in the same cupboard
12.w: Original labelled containers help preserve identification, instructions and safe handling information.

n.0: Better than an unmarked container, but the original label carries the full hazard information.
n.1: Secure storage is good; removing hazard labels defeats the point.
n.3: Grouping by colour can place incompatible chemicals side by side.
n.4: Sheets should be accessible, but storing paper with chemicals risks contaminating them.

12.q: When item 12 is used, why should the orange shield be positioned correctly?
o: To improve retention of the impression tray
To increase the etching effect on enamel
To prevent the composite from becoming too cold
To reduce exposure to the intense blue curing light
To stop alginate setting too quickly
12.w: The orange shield helps protect eyes from the intense blue light emitted during curing.

n.0: Tray retention depends on fit and impression material handling, not the curing light shield.
n.2: The shield does not control composite temperature.
n.1: Etching is performed chemically, not by the shield.
n.4: Alginate setting is unrelated to the curing light shield.

12.q: A colleague calls for help because a patient has collapsed in the waiting room. Which item is most important to bring first when responding to a collapsed patient elsewhere in the practice?
o: Emergency drugs kit and AED if available
12.w: Emergency response equipment such as the AED and emergency kit should be prioritised.

n.0: Administrative items are not immediate priorities.
n.3: Routine dental instruments are not first-line emergency equipment.
n.4: These may help later but are not priorities.
n.2: Impression materials are unrelated.

12.q: Referral letters and laboratory sheets accumulate at reception during a busy clinic. Which sequence best reflects safe handling of confidential paperwork?
o: Collect it promptly, store securely, dispose of it appropriately when no longer needed
Collect it promptly, store securely, then archive every document indefinitely
File it at the end of the week and shred anything left over
Keep it on the desk while in use, then file it at the end of the day
Scan it immediately, then place the paper in the general waste
12.w: Confidential documents should be controlled, securely stored and disposed of through approved methods.

n.1: Keeping everything indefinitely conflicts with retention policy.
n.2: Leaves identifiable information unsecured for days.
n.3: A whole day on an open desk is a confidentiality risk.
n.4: The scanning is fine; general waste is the wrong disposal route.

12.q: A periapical radiograph of the lower molar region shows the apices visible but a radiopaque band crossing the lower part of the image. What is the most likely explanation for this appearance?
o: Cone cut due to poor beam alignment
Periapical pathology affecting the mandibular molar roots
The patient’s finger or receptor holder has been superimposed on the image
12.w: A distinct radiopaque band crossing part of the image is most consistent with superimposition of a finger, holder component or other external object during exposure.

n.2: Periapical pathology appears around root apices, not as a straight radiopaque band across the image.
n.4: Mandibular cortex anatomy would not present as an isolated superimposed band.
n.1: Chemical fog reduces contrast more generally rather than creating a defined radiopaque strip.
n.0: Cone cut creates an unexposed pale or white area, not a dense superimposed band.

12.q: Based on the image, which stage of caries is shown?
12.w: The cavitation and depth indicate advanced dentine involvement.

12.q: A pack is examined after the cycle has finished. Which item is being identified as a post-cycle monitoring aid?

n.2: Tray liners are disposed of during dirty stages.
n.1: Dirty instruments start the workflow.

12.q: The final suture has been placed following a surgical extraction. What is the best sequence once suturing is complete?

n.1: The surgery should be made safe before dismissal.
n.4: Alginate impressions are unrelated.

12.q: Interpret the lesion shown in the image.
o: A benign mucocele of the lower lip
A normal variation of the dorsal tongue
A physiological fissure of the tongue
A simple coating of the tongue surface
A suspicious ulcerative lesion requiring urgent investigation
12.w: The lesion is ulcerative, irregular and clinically suspicious, so it requires urgent investigation.

n.1: Normal variation would not present as a destructive irregular ulcer.
n.0: A mucocele typically affects minor salivary gland sites such as the lip and has a different appearance.
n.2: A fissured tongue does not present as a red-white ulcerated lesion.
n.3: A tongue coating is superficial and does not produce this ulcerated appearance.

12.q: A patient telephones a few hours after an extraction. Which sign after extraction should be reported promptly to the clinician?
12.w: Persistent bleeding requires prompt review and management.

n.0: Temporary numbness may relate to anaesthetic early on.
n.3: Taste alone is not urgent.
n.2: Mild tiredness may be nonspecific.
n.4: Minor fullness can occur postoperatively.

12.q: New agency staff are due to start in the decontamination room. Which sign would most help temporary staff maintain zones?
12.w: Clear clean and dirty area signs help staff identify where items should and should not be placed.

n.0: Break rotas do not guide zoning.
n.4: Wi-Fi details are unrelated.
n.2: Parking maps do not support decontamination control.
n.3: Uniform lists do not identify zones.

12.q: A dental nurse notices the image has overlapped premolar contacts but clearer molar contacts. Which interpretation is most accurate?
o: Exposure time was too short only in the premolar region
Horizontal angulation was slightly incorrect and centred away from premolar contacts
The patient moved only the premolars
12.w: Partial overlap in one region suggests beam alignment was slightly off-centre, missing some contact points while others remained open.

n.1: Exposure time affects the whole image, not one region selectively.
n.4: A reversed receptor would create a characteristic pattern across the image.
n.3: Movement does not isolate only premolar contacts in this way.
n.0: Processing faults affect image quality globally.

12.q: Which feature in the image most strongly indicates positioning error rather than angulation error?
o: The lower root tips extend beyond the image border
12.w: When anatomy is simply excluded from the receptor area, this most strongly indicates positioning error.

n.4: Unusually long teeth would suggest elongation.
n.0: Overlapped contacts suggest horizontal angulation error.
n.2: Blur indicates movement.
n.1: Crown density changes do not indicate positioning specifically.

12.q: A glass slab is not dried before cement mixing, and moisture remains on the surface. Why is this poor equipment preparation?
o: Extra moisture can alter the intended powder-liquid ratio and handling
It guarantees a longer working time without affecting properties
It makes the cement more radiopaque
It prevents the cement from adhering to the restoration
It will improve the film thickness automatically
12.w: Residual moisture can change the mix consistency and affect the setting characteristics of moisture-sensitive cements.

n.4: Film thickness is not predictably improved by contamination with water.
n.2: Radiopacity is not determined by surface moisture.
n.3: Adhesion effects are not the primary issue described here.
n.1: Although handling may change, the properties are not reliably preserved.

12.q: A patient presents with exposed root surfaces due to recession. What is the best action to reduce sensitivity?
12.w: Desensitising agents help block dentinal tubules and reduce sensitivity.

n.3: Enamel polishing does not address exposed roots.
n.4: Removing dentine worsens sensitivity.
n.1: Extraction is unnecessary for sensitivity alone.
n.2: Increased brushing can worsen recession.

12.q: During an oral examination, a structure is identified as forming the anterior roof of the mouth and consisting of bone. What is this structure?
12.w: The hard palate forms the anterior bony roof of the oral cavity.

n.2: The soft palate is posterior and not bony.
n.4: The uvula is a soft tissue extension of the soft palate.
n.3: The tongue is located on the floor of the mouth.
n.0: The floor of the mouth is inferior, not part of the roof.

12.q: A patient returns the day after periodontal instrumentation reporting soreness. Which sign most suggests trauma from over-instrumentation after treatment?
12.w: Soft tissue laceration suggests traumatic instrumentation.

n.2: Reduced plaque score is beneficial, not traumatic.
n.0: Taste does not indicate trauma.
n.1: Blood pressure is unrelated.
n.3: Occlusion is unrelated here.

12.q: A dental nurse incorrectly records a lower right canine as 43. What is the correct FDI number?
12.w: The lower right canine is correctly recorded as 43, so there is no error.

n.2: 33 refers to the lower left canine.
n.0: 13 refers to the upper right canine.
n.1: 23 refers to the upper left canine.
n.4: 44 refers to the lower right first premolar.

12.q: A nervous patient says they never understand dental advice because too much information is given at once. What is the best approach?
o: Give one clear message at a time
Provide all advice as one lecture
12.w: Breaking advice into clear manageable points improves understanding and recall.

n.4: Technical language may reduce understanding.
n.2: Too much information at once can overwhelm patients.
n.3: Speaking faster may reduce comprehension.
n.0: Questions help clarify understanding and should be encouraged.

12.q: A relative telephones asking what treatment a patient received. Which statement best describes confidentiality in dental practice?
o: It ends once treatment is complete
It is optional if the practice is busy
Patient information should be protected and shared only appropriately
12.w: Confidentiality requires protecting personal information and limiting disclosure to appropriate circumstances.

n.3: Many forms of patient information are confidential, not only notes.
n.0: It applies to all patients.
n.1: Duties continue after treatment ends.
n.2: Workload does not remove confidentiality duties.

12.q: A lower third molar is being removed surgically with a bur and irrigation. Why is suction particularly important during a surgical extraction?
12.w: Suction removes blood and fluids to maintain visibility for the operator.

n.4: Suction does not whiten teeth.
n.1: Pulp size is unaffected.
n.3: Sutures are not strengthened by suction.
n.2: Instrument sterilisation occurs separately.

12.q: A busy clinic is running short of bench space. Which practice most clearly breaks one-way workflow principles?
o: Returning dirty trays through clean side
12.w: Dirty items should not pass back through the clean side once segregation routes are established.

n.1: Moving dirty items to the sink is expected.
n.2: Drying cleaned items can be appropriate.
n.3: Labelling clean shelves supports organisation.
n.0: Date checking supports stock control.

12.q: A wax try-in has been assessed with the patient and the clinician. What is the best sequence after trying in a denture for fit and appearance?
12.w: Any required changes should be clearly recorded for the next stage.

n.3: Further planning is needed before dismissal.
n.0: The denture should not be discarded.
n.4: Forceps are unrelated.
n.1: Plaster mixing is not the immediate clinical step.

12.q: Examine the radiograph. Which limitation is most associated with this radiographic type?
o: Excessive radiation dose compared to all other techniques
High level of image distortion and reduced detail compared to intraoral radiographs
Restricted view limited to posterior teeth only
12.w: Panoramic radiographs provide a broad overview but have lower resolution and increased distortion compared to intraoral radiographs.

n.3: Root apices are visible on panoramic radiographs, though with less detail.
n.4: Panoramic images include the full dentition, not just posterior teeth.
n.2: Bone levels can be assessed, though less precisely than with bitewings.
n.0: Panoramic radiographs do not necessarily have the highest radiation dose compared to all techniques.

12.q: A practice is redesigning its decontamination room. Which arrangement best supports one-way decontamination workflow?
o: Dirty intake to clean storage sequence
12.w: A clear progression from dirty intake through processing to clean storage supports safe one-way flow.

n.3: Sink areas are unsuitable for sterile stock.
n.2: Mixed benches increase contamination risk.
n.4: Waste should be separated from clean items.
n.0: Crossing routes undermine segregation.

12.q: The image shows a cavitated lesion. Which term best describes this stage?
12.w: Cavitation indicates dentine involvement and irreversible damage.

n.4: Reversible lesions are non-cavitated.
n.3: Initial caries does not involve cavitation.
n.0: Arrested lesions are inactive.
n.2: This is not a healthy surface.

12.q: A patient says they brush immediately after frequent fizzy drinks because they want to protect their teeth. Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Brush harder immediately after each drink
Delay brushing for a period after acidic drinks and rinse with water first
Skip all brushing on days acidic drinks are taken
Use a medium brush and scrub affected areas
Use mouthwash straight after the drink instead of brushing ever again
12.w: Brushing immediately after acid exposure may increase wear; delaying and rinsing first is preferable.

n.0: Immediate vigorous brushing may increase erosive wear.
n.4: Mouthwash does not replace normal toothbrushing.
n.2: Regular brushing should continue with sensible timing.
n.3: Scrubbing after acid exposure is not recommended.

12.q: Clean and dirty trays have been mixed and their status is now uncertain. Which action best restores zone control after accidental mixing of clean and dirty trays?
o: Ask the team what they remember about each tray
Continue but process both trays again at the end
Re-label the trays and monitor more closely
Treat the mixed items as clean and use them first
12.w: The process should stop so trays can be separated and any compromised items assessed.

n.0: Recollection is not a substitute for assessment.
n.1: Reprocessing later does not help the patient treated in the meantime.
n.2: Labels record a decision that has not yet been made.
n.4: Assumes the safest outcome without any basis.

12.q: During CPR, the chest is not returning fully to its normal position between compressions. What is the error that should be corrected?
o: Leaning on the chest between compressions
12.w: Leaning prevents full chest recoil, reducing venous return and CPR effectiveness.

n.0: Frequent changes can be managed well and do not specifically cause poor recoil.
n.4: Early AED use is beneficial, not the issue described.
n.3: Oxygen timing does not explain lack of recoil.
n.1: Counting aloud may help coordination and is not the error shown.

12.q: A Class II restoration is being prepared and the dentist asks for the device that secures a matrix band around the tooth. Which instrument type is needed?
12.w: A matrix retainer holds and tightens a matrix band around the tooth during restoration placement.

n.0: An amalgam well is a container used to hold mixed amalgam.
n.1: A dappen dish holds small amounts of liquid or paste.
n.2: An excavator is used to remove soft carious dentine.
n.4: A shade guide is used for colour matching.

12.q: A patient is being dismissed after having a molar extracted. Which postoperative advice is most appropriate after extraction?
12.w: Avoiding rinsing initially helps protect the forming clot.

n.3: Smoking increases complication risk.
n.4: Suction from straws may disturb the clot.
n.1: Vigorous exercise may increase bleeding.
n.2: Touching the socket can disrupt healing.

12.q: From the image, which structure lies directly beneath enamel?
12.w: Dentine forms the bulk of the tooth and lies directly under enamel.

n.4: The pulp is deeper.
n.1: Cementum is on the root.
n.3: Gingiva is external soft tissue.

12.q: A team member wears long artificial nails under gloves. Why is this poor PPE practice?

n.0: Grip is not the infection-control concern.
n.2: Apron fastening is unrelated.
n.3: Nails do not directly determine mask fit.

12.q: Bags are stacked temporarily in a corridor while awaiting collection. What is the main risk of leaving waste bags in an evacuation route?
o: They may obstruct escape and create hazards

n.1: Appearance is not the main safety concern.
n.4: Internet speed is unrelated.
n.0: They do not improve ventilation meaningfully.
n.3: Contracts are not the principal issue.

12.q: A patient returns two weeks after receiving a new lower denture. Which finding most strongly suggests poor denture retention?
12.w: Movement during function often indicates poor retention or stability.

n.3: A shiny surface does not indicate retention quality.
n.2: Pink acrylic colour is normal.
n.0: Clasps alone do not confirm poor retention.
n.4: Storage location is unrelated.

12.q: A patient becomes unresponsive in the waiting area, is not breathing normally, and no pulse is detected. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Begin chest compressions and call for the AED
Check the pulse again for a full minute
Give high-flow oxygen and observe for response
Move the patient to the dental chair before acting
Place the patient in the recovery position

n.4: Recovery position is only appropriate for a breathing unconscious patient.
n.2: Oxygen may be helpful later, but delaying compressions reduces survival chances.
n.1: Pulse checks should be brief; prolonged reassessment delays CPR.

12.q: The practice is arranging its quarterly removal of clinical material. Which record is most useful when arranging licensed waste collection?
